appearance: The Centzon Totochtin were generally depicted as rabbits or anthropomorphic figures with rabbit ears and features. Their attire often included elements associated with pulque, such as maguey leaves or vessels containing the fermented drink. They were often portrayed in scenes of celebration and intoxication.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: The Centzon Totochtin were born from the union of Mayahuel, the goddess of the maguey plant, and Patecatl, a god associated with medicine and pulque. Mayahuel, often depicted with numerous breasts to nourish her many children, provided the source of pulque, while Patecatl contributed to its creation and ritualistic use. The number '400' signifies a vast and diverse group of deities, each embodying different facets of intoxication. Myths surrounding the Centzon Totochtin often involve stories of their mischievous antics, their role in promoting revelry and celebration, and their connection to the spiritual and visionary aspects of pulque consumption.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: The Centzon Totochtin played a crucial role in Aztec society, as pulque consumption was deeply ingrained in ritualistic and social practices. Pulque was not merely a recreational beverage but was also used in religious ceremonies, festivals, and healing rituals. The Centzon Totochtin were invoked during these occasions to ensure a successful and spiritually enriching experience. Their presence symbolized the transformative power of intoxication, which could lead to heightened awareness, creativity, and connection with the divine. However, excessive consumption was frowned upon, and the Centzon Totochtin also served as a reminder of the potential dangers of uncontrolled drunkenness.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: The Centzon Totochtin symbolize the multifaceted nature of intoxication, encompassing both its positive and negative aspects. The rabbit, as their animal representation, often embodies fertility, abundance, and playfulness, reflecting the celebratory and social dimensions of pulque consumption. The number '400' emphasizes the vast array of experiences and emotions associated with drunkenness, from euphoria and camaraderie to disorientation and recklessness. The Centzon Totochtin can be interpreted as a reminder of the importance of balance and moderation in all aspects of life, particularly in the pursuit of pleasure and altered states of consciousness.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: While the Aztec empire fell to Spanish conquistadors, and many indigenous religious practices were suppressed, the cultural significance of pulque and the memory of the Centzon Totochtin have persisted in modern Mexico. Pulque continues to be produced and consumed, particularly in rural areas, and it is experiencing a resurgence in popularity among younger generations seeking to reconnect with their cultural heritage. The Centzon Totochtin are sometimes referenced in contemporary art, literature, and music as symbols of indigenous identity, cultural resistance, and the enduring power of ancient traditions. They represent a connection to a pre-Columbian past and a celebration of the unique cultural heritage of Mexico.

name: Centzon Totochtin
shortDescription: The Centzon Totochtin were the 400 rabbit gods of drunkenness in Aztec mythology, associated with pulque, the fermented beverage.
description: The Centzon Totochtin, meaning 'Four Hundred Rabbits,' represent the collective of rabbit gods associated with pulque, a fermented alcoholic beverage made from the maguey plant, in Aztec mythology. These deities were not individually named, but rather represented different aspects and manifestations of drunkenness and revelry. They were children of Mayahuel, the goddess of the maguey plant, and Patecatl, a god associated with medicine and pulque. The number '400' in Nahuatl, the Aztec language, often symbolized innumerability, implying a vast and diverse group of deities embodying the various ways one could become intoxicated. They played a significant role in Aztec social and religious life, as pulque consumption was a ritualistic practice.
